name: template-script
intent: Make the view file itself the program: the page script reads request parameters, obtains the model data it needs and writes the response markup, so a page can ship with no separate controller, presentation model or helper layer.
problem: A dynamic page needs data from the model and markup around it, and the team does not want the ceremony of a controller that selects an action, gathers the data and forwards to a template. The shortest path is to let the page fetch what it needs while it renders - so the recurring decision is whether the page file may own the request end to end (JSP Model 1) or whether a thin handler should prepare the data first and leave the view to make markers.
context: Server-side rendering where the page artifact is executed per request (JSP/ASP.NET/ERB/EJS-style scriptlets, or a handler that emits markup directly), where the model is reachable from the view's own process (DAO, repository, service locator, request-scoped beans) and where page count and traffic are small enough that duplicated data access and an untestable view remain affordable.
benefits: Fewest moving parts per page: no controller, no presentation model, no helper layer - the page is handler and template in one artifact, which is why the JSP world named it Model 1.
Shortest path to a working dynamic page: one file to create, deploy and read, and no wiring to design before the first request renders.
Data shaping happens where the markup is written, so ad-hoc pages (admin screens, diagnostics, one-off reports) can render exactly the fields they happen to have without first designing a DTO.
The script inherits the container's page lifecycle: request, response, session, authentication state and error pages are already in scope, so cross-cutting context needs no plumbing.
For a genuinely single-page workflow, parameter extraction, data lookup and markup stay visible in one place, which keeps small changes cheap to make.
tradeoffs: Data access is welded into the view: the page cannot be exercised without a container and a model, so its logic is not unit-testable and its bugs are found by rendering.
The same fetch-and-format logic is copy-pasted from page to page; changing a query or a rule means editing every page that embeds it.
Every interpolation is an escaping decision its author can get wrong; one missing escape is a cross-site-scripting hole, and engines protect only the paths that go through their escape function.
The view is source code: designers and content authors lose their ability to maintain the markup, which removes the main advantage a template had over hand-written output.
Serving a second channel (JSON, mobile, email) means re-implementing the page's logic elsewhere or extracting it under pressure later.
A slow or failing model call surfaces as a half-written response, because the script has usually started writing markup before the failure arrives.
Container-compiled pages (JSP, .aspx) surface syntax and markup errors on the first request rather than at build time, and each page keeps its own compiled artifact and cache entry.

participants.responsibility: The executed view file: it extracts request parameters, obtains the model data it needs, drives loops and conditionals, and interleaves the results with literal template text.
Whatever lets the script reach domain data - DAO or repository, service locator, request-scoped bean, or an HTTP client - called straight from the view instead of from a service boundary.
The write path that turns evaluated expressions and template text into the response stream (the JSP writer, Razor's output buffer, ERB's output buffer, or a printf-family sink).
Request, response and session objects supplied by the server runtime, used for input, authentication state and cross-request state that the script reads without declaring a dependency on it.
The container or engine that loads, compiles, caches and executes the page script per request, and that reports its errors as responses.

use_cases: Admin, diagnostic and back-office pages that read a handful of fields and print them, where a controller/DTO split would be pure ceremony.
Legacy JSP, ASP.NET or ERB pages in production whose Model 1 structure is being maintained or migrated incrementally rather than rewritten in one step.
One-off generated reports and printable pages where a single pass over query results produces the whole artifact.
Prototypes that must demonstrate a workflow end to end before a controller and presentation layer are designed.
Internal tooling dashboards with a small page count and one audience (the team), where velocity beats structure.

Plain PHP applications: the manual's own model is a .php file interleaving HTML with <?php ?> blocks, reading $_GET/$_POST from the request and fetching the data it prints (the manual names htmlspecialchars() as the escaping step for output) - the page-as-script arrangement as the shipped default, not a deviation from it.

WordPress classic themes: template files are PHP files chosen per request by the Template Hierarchy, and The Loop queries and iterates posts inside the view file itself while template tags print each field - a production page-script at enormous scale, maintained rather than rewritten.

Classic ASP pages on current IIS: the server separates <% %> script blocks from the static HTML, executes them (database access and Response writes from within the page) and injects the results into the reply; Microsoft documents Classic ASP as still first-class on modern IIS, so these Model 1 pages are maintained in place.
avoid_when: The page's logic is worth testing or reusing: put a thin Page Controller in front and render a Template View, which shrinks the page to markers and makes the data boundary mockable.
The view needs formatting or selection logic: move it into a View Helper (bean, tag or helper method) so the markup stays declarative and the helper is testable on its own.
The output is consumed by machines (JSON, XML, CSV): a Transform View walking the domain data is the honest structure - there is no markup to interleave with code.
Many requests produce the same response: generate it once and serve it from a Page Cache instead of re-running a script per request.
More than one channel must render the same data: prepare a presentation model once and render it per channel (Two-Step View, Multiple Views) rather than duplicating the script.
anti_patterns: Business rules and transactions inside the page script, so the view becomes the only implementation of the application's logic (the Model 1 failure mode).
Unescaped interpolation of user-controlled data - the scriptlet path that produces stored and reflected XSS.
One page owning request handling, data access, presentation and navigation decisions at once, so every change risks breaking all four.
Growing by duplication: cloning the page for each new case instead of extracting a helper, a partial or a shared template.
Hand-rolling HTML as string concatenation in a runtime that already ships a template facility - reinventing the engine, badly and without escaping.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: this pattern knowingly trades it away - presentation, data access and control flow meet in one artifact, so the boundary has to be watched deliberately.
Single responsibility: a page script that also owns business rules violates it, and that is exactly the line to draw when deciding what stays in the page.
Information hiding: the markup should not know how data is stored, but a script that queries directly leaks the storage model into the view.
Open/closed: a new rendering channel or a changed query should not force edits to every existing page.
best_practices: Keep the script to the page's own concerns: read parameters, obtain already-shaped data, emit markup - push rules, transactions and caching behind a service or DAO call.

Route every dynamic value through the engine's escaping path (<%= %>, @expression, {{ }}, #( )) and treat raw or unescaped output (<%- %>, HtmlHelper.Raw, #unsafeHTML, |safe) as an exception that must be justified in review.
Give each page exactly one entry point for model access, so the fetch has a single place to change when the query or the schema moves.
Bound the script's size: when a page needs more than a screenful of logic, extract a View Helper or give that page a controller instead of growing the script.
Set the response content type and charset before any output and validate the request first, so failures produce a clean error response rather than a truncated page.
Extract the decisions worth testing (filtering, formatting, permission checks) out of the page and leave the script with calls and literals.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003), Ch. 14 'Web Presentation Patterns' - Template View, Transform View and Two Step View define the family this pattern belongs to and the structures it competes with; https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/templateView.html

Qusay H. Mahmoud, 'Servlets and JSP Pages Best Practices', Oracle (2003) - describes JSP Model 1 (the page processes the request and builds the reply) and warns that embedded scriptlets produce applications that are hard to reuse, enhance and maintain; https://www.oracle.com/technical-resources/articles/javase/servlets-jsp.html

Jakarta Server Pages 3.1 specification (2022) - a JSP page interleaves template data with dynamic actions and supports scripting elements; scripts 'glue together this functionality in a per-page manner'; https://jakarta.ee/specifications/pages/3.1/jakarta-server-pages-spec-3.1

Andrew Patzer, 'Foundations of JSP design patterns: The View Helper pattern' (InfoWorld excerpt, 2004) - from a page you may embed scriptlets, use the expression language, or use a helper; helpers are the documented remedy for logic (and Java) inside the view; https://www.infoworld.com/article/2165763/java-web-development-foundations-of-jsp-design-patterns-the-view-helper-pattern.html

JSP model 1 architecture (Wikipedia) - a JSP page handling processing, validation, business logic and response generation duplicates functionality in every page and ties business logic to presentation, which is why adding a second view means duplicating it; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSP_model_1_architecture

PHP Manual, 'PHP and HTML' (php.net) - the page itself retrieves $_GET/$_POST from the request and generates the surrounding HTML, with htmlspecialchars() named as the escaping routine for values written into attributes: the page-as-script form as PHP's documented default; https://www.php.net/html/

Microsoft Learn, 'ASP Overview' (IIS 6.0 SDK) - an .asp file is HTML plus server-side script in <% %> delimiters; IIS separates the script blocks, executes them (including database access) and injects the output into the page sent via the Response object; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/iis/6.0-sdk/ms524929(v=vs.90)

WordPress Theme Handbook, 'Template Files' and 'The Loop' - classic theme templates are PHP files selected per request by the Template Hierarchy, and the template file itself runs The Loop to retrieve and format posts while template tags print each field; https://developer.wordpress.org/themes/classic-themes/basics/template-files/ ; https://developer.wordpress.org/themes/classic-themes/basics/the-loop/

OWASP, 'Cross Site Scripting Prevention' Cheat Sheet - every untrusted value must be encoded for its output context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL) at the point of output; one unencoded interpolation in a page script makes stored and reflected XSS, the pattern's dominant real-world failure; https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

MDN, 'GET request method' - GET is safe, idempotent and cacheable and must never change server state, because browsers, caches and prefetchers re-issue it without user intent; grounds why a page script must not write state while rendering a GET; https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods/GET
